title: Action de Galois sur Teichmüller : notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
Context (pages 23-25). Grothendieck builds a rigid, S_3-symmetric combinatorial model of the profinite fundamental groupoid of P^1 minus {0,1,∞}, here written Σ_J with J = {0,1,∞}.

The model:
- Six base points R_i^ω, with i ∈ J and ω ∈ {ω, ω'}, the two cyclic orders on J. These play the role of tangential base points near each puncture.
- Half-loops a_i^ω : R_i^ω → R_i^{ω'}, with a_i^{ω'} a_i^ω = λ_i^ω = φ_i^ω(l_0), a loop around the puncture i.
- Connecting arcs b_i^ω, later modified to b̃_i^ω = a b.
- Group G_J ≅ S_3, acting simply transitively on these arcs.
- Complex conjugation τ.
- Identifications φ_i^ω : π̂_{0,3} = ⟨l_0, l_1, l_∞ | l_∞ l_1 l_0 = 1⟩ → π_1(Σ, R_i^ω).
- Automorphisms ε_0 (with ε_0^2 = l_0), σ_∞ (swapping l_0 and l_1), and the rotation ρ (l_0 → l_1 → l_∞ → l_0), with ρ^{-1} = ε_0 σ_∞.
- Relations (2a) b b' = 1 and (2b), a hexagon-type relation, rewritten as (8)/(9) b̃ b̃ b̃ = 1.

This page. Let u be an automorphism of the system of profinite quasi-groupoids Î_J that:
- commutes with Ĝ_J,
- fixes the base points,
- respects the sub-quasi-groupoids Î_{J,i} generated by the a_i^ω and b̃_i^ω.

On the local pieces u must act by u(a_i^ω) = a_i^ω φ(l_0^γ), with γ ∈ Ẑ independent of i and ω. Then u(λ_i^ω) = (λ_i^ω)^{2γ+1}. So ρ := 2γ+1 ∈ Ẑ^* is the 'multiplicateur', i.e. the cyclotomic character (Drinfeld's λ), and γ = (ρ−1)/2 (Drinfeld's m). On the connecting arcs u(b̃_i^ω) = b̃_i^ω φ_{ω'i}(β), with β ∈ π̂_{0,3] (Drinfeld's f).

The pair (ρ, β) determines u; Grothendieck adds that in fact β determines ρ. Transporting the defining relations of the groupoid ((2a) and the hexagon (8)/(9)) under u gives conditions (12):
- (I) β σ_∞(β) = 1, i.e. f(x,y) f(y,x) = 1.
- (II) α ρ^{-1}(α) ρ^{-2}(α) = 1, where α = l_1^γ β and ρ is now the rotation.

Expanding (II) gives, up to conjugation, β(l_0,l_1) l_0^γ β(l_∞,l_0) l_∞^γ β(l_1,l_∞) l_1^γ = 1. This is exactly Drinfeld's hexagon relation f(x,y) x^m f(z,x) z^m f(y,z) y^m = 1, with m = (λ−1)/2. The product convention here is l_∞ l_1 l_0 = 1 rather than xyz = 1. Grothendieck's NB says that replacing β by β^{-1} and α by α^{-1} recovers 'les équations habituelles', so he already had the standard form elsewhere.

So the page derives the two defining relations (I) and (II) of the profinite Grothendieck-Teichmüller group ĜT (without the pentagon relation III, which needs M_{0,5}). They come out as the conditions for an automorphism of the S_3-equivariant genus-0 groupoid with six base points.

The last paragraph addresses the conjugate τ u τ^{-1}. It is given by (ρ, σ_∞(β)). Grothendieck asks for a direct verification, by computation in π̂_{0,3}, that (12) for β implies (12) for β' = σ_∞(β) with the same γ. This is the compatibility of the 'GT' conditions with complex conjugation; in modern terms, conjugation by the element (−1, 1).

The margins:
- note that he should first justify why u(a) has the form a·φ(λ^γ);
- worry whether u is determined by (ρ, β);
- discuss how the equations change if β is redefined as σ_∞(β).
errors: Notational clash: ρ denotes both the multiplicateur in Ẑ^* and the order-3 rotation automorphism of π̂_{0,3} (ρ^{-1} = ε_0 σ_∞) within the same equations (12). The meaning must be read from context.
The line u(λ_i^ω a_i^ω) = φ(l_0^{2γ}… l_0) is garbled. The correct statement is u(λ_i^ω) = u(a_i^{ω'}) u(a_i^ω) = (λ_i^ω)^{2γ+1}, using that a_i^ω commutes with powers of λ. This gives ρ = 2γ+1.
γ = (ρ−1)/2 ∈ Ẑ requires ρ − 1 ∈ 2Ẑ. This holds for every ρ ∈ Ẑ^*: the 2-adic component is odd, and 2 is invertible at the other primes. So there is no actual gap, but it is unstated.

The claim 'β détermine ρ' is asserted without proof. Abelianizing (II) gives no information on γ, because x^γ y^γ z^γ abelianizes to γ(x+y+z) = 0. So this claim needs a genuine argument and remains unverified on the page.

The step 'u(a) = a·φ(l_0^γ) with γ independent of i, ω' is acknowledged in the margin as still needing justification. It follows from S_3-equivariance and the centralizer of the half-loop, but that argument is not given.

ideas.what: Profinite automorphisms of an S_3-equivariant fundamental groupoid of P^1−{0,1,∞} with six (tangential-type) base points, parametrized by a pair (ρ, β) ∈ Ẑ^* × π̂_{0,3}
ideas.modern_name: Grothendieck-Teichmüller group ĜT, with elements (λ, f)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Drinfeld (1990, 'On quasitriangular quasi-Hopf algebras and a group closely connected with Gal(Q̄/Q)'); Ihara (1990-91)
ideas.where_published: Esquisse d'un programme (1984) only describes the program (Teichmüller tower determined by levels 1-2, Galois action via automorphisms of the tower); it gives no explicit equations

ideas.what: Relation α ρ^{-1}(α) ρ^{-2}(α) = 1 with α = l_1^{(ρ−1)/2} β
ideas.modern_name: GT hexagon relation (II): f(x,y) x^m f(z,x) z^m f(y,z) y^m = 1, m = (λ−1)/2

ideas.what: Multiplicateur ρ = 2γ+1 acting on the local monodromy λ_i by raising to the power ρ
Action of complex conjugation τ on u: τ u τ^{-1} corresponds to (ρ, σ_∞(β)); request to verify that (12) is stable under β ↦ σ_∞(β)
ideas.modern_name: compatibility of ĜT with complex conjugation; centralizer of c = (−1,1) in ĜT

ideas.what: Six base points with half-loops a_i^ω (a_i^{ω'} a_i^ω = local loop) and square root ε_0 (ε_0^2 = l_0)
ideas.modern_name: tangential base points / 'half-turns' in genus-0 groupoid; Ihara-Deligne tangential base points
ideas.where_published: Esquisse mentions base points on the 'soft' boundary informally

missed.claim: Explicit derivation of the two genus-0, 3-point defining relations of ĜT, (I) f(x,y)f(y,x) = 1 and (II) the hexagon with exponent m = (λ−1)/2, for pairs (λ, f) ∈ Ẑ^* × π̂_{0,3}. They arise as the conditions for an automorphism of an S_3-equivariant groupoid with six base points. This predates Drinfeld and Ihara (1990), apparently by about a decade.
missed.quote: β σ_∞(β) = 1 ; α ρ^{-1}(α) ρ^{-2}(α) = 1 ; α = l_1^γ β … γ = (ρ−1)/2, ρ ∈ Ẑ^* multiplicateur
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is direct documentary evidence that Grothendieck had the explicit ĜT equations (I) and (II), including the (λ−1)/2 exponent. They are usually attributed to Drinfeld and Ihara. It is relevant for the attribution and history of ĜT, and it shows a groupoid/'quasi-groupoïde' derivation via S_3-equivariance and half-loops rather than via quasi-Hopf algebras.

missed.claim: Grothendieck asks for a direct algebraic verification inside π̂_{0,3} that relations (12) for β imply the same relations for β' = σ_∞(β), with the same γ. This is the complex-conjugation symmetry of the GT equations.
missed.quote: Il faudrait pouvoir vérifier directement, par un calcul dans π_{0,3}, que les équations (12) sur β, impliquent les mêmes relations pour β' = σ_∞(β)
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is essentially known now: conjugation by (−1,1) preserves ĜT. But the explicit direct computation from (I) and (II) alone is a small, clean exercise that is rarely written out.

missed.claim: Assertion that β alone determines the multiplicateur ρ, given here without proof.
missed.quote: Ici (ρ,β) détermine u (en fait, β détermine ρ..)
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Whether f determines λ for (λ, f) satisfying only (I) and (II) is a precise question. Abelianization of (II) is uninformative, so a proof would require a finer argument. It is worth checking against the literature on ĜT.

deep.surprise_reason: The page contains, explicitly and correctly, the two ĜT relations (I) and (II) with the characteristic exponent (λ−1)/2, written in an undated manuscript (from 1978 onward). The NB's reference to 'les équations habituelles' indicates these were already familiar to him. The published record credits the equations to Drinfeld and Ihara (1990); the Esquisse gives no formulas. Specialists aware of the archive (e.g. Schneps) may already know Grothendieck anticipated this, which tempers the score. The pentagon relation is absent.
transcription_corrections: In the first displayed relation, the image reads u(a_i^ω) = a_i^ω φ_{iω}(l_0^γ) = φ_i^ω(l_0^γ) a_i^ω, with the side note 'l_0^γ indépendant des i,ω, γ ∈ Ẑ'.
The garbled line is probably u(λ_i^{ω'}… a_i^ω) = φ_{iω}(l_0^{2γ} l_0), i.e. it gives λ^{2γ+1}.
In (12) the third line is α = l_1^γ β with underbrace σ_∞(λ); the crossed-out version 'α = l_1^{-γ} β' appears to the right, next to 'où'.
The NB at right reads roughly: 'NB Si on remplace β par β^{-1}, α par α^{-1}, on retrouve les équations habituelles (α^{-1} ρ(α^{-1}) ρ^2(α^{-1}) = 1) cf plus loin'.
The margin near the bottom reads: 'Si on change de définition de β, en le remplaçant par σ_∞(β), β devient … dans les deux premières équations (12) … α = l_1 σ_∞(β) …'.
Inline after the system: '(= φ_{ω'i}(σ_∞ β) b̃_i^ω)'.
In the final line, 'ζ_∞(β)' is σ_∞(β).
